title: Steel Column with Buckling and Fire Resistance
prompt:
Select the lightest standard hot-rolled steel H-section (from the European HE series or equivalent universal column series) for an interior column in a 6-storey office building, satisfying both ambient-temperature buckling resistance AND 60-minute fire resistance without applied fire protection.

Design data:
- Column height (storey height): 4.0 m, pinned at both ends (effective length factor = 1.0).
- Axial load: 2800 kN ultimate limit state (ULS) factored load at ambient temperature.
- Fire load: 1680 kN (fire limit state, using load reduction factor η_fi = 0.6 applied to the ambient ULS load).
- Steel grade: S355 (f_y = 355 MPa at ambient temperature).
- Fire resistance requirement: R60 (60 minutes) to EN 1993-1-2.
- The column is unprotected (no intumescent paint, no board, no spray).

Your design must address:

Part 1 — AMBIENT DESIGN (EN 1993-1-1):
1. For each candidate section, calculate the slenderness ratio λ = L_eff / r_min where r_min is the minimum radius of gyration.
2. Determine the non-dimensional slenderness λ̄ = (L_eff / r_min) × (1/π) × √(f_y / E), where E = 210,000 MPa.
3. Select the appropriate buckling curve (a, b, c, or d) based on the section geometry and axis of buckling (use curve b for HE sections with h/b ≤ 1.2 buckling about the weak axis, curve a for h/b > 1.2).
4. Calculate the buckling reduction factor χ from the European column curves using the imperfection factor α.
5. Verify N_b,Rd = χ × A × f_y / γ_M1 ≥ 2800 kN, where γ_M1 = 1.0.

Part 2 — FIRE DESIGN (EN 1993-1-2):
1. Calculate the section factor A_m/V for the unprotected section (exposed perimeter / cross-sectional area). For a column exposed on all four sides, A_m = the full perimeter of the cross-section.
2. Using the simplified temperature-time method or the critical temperature approach:
   a. Calculate the degree of utilisation μ_0 = N_fi,Ed / N_fi,Rd,0, where N_fi,Ed = 1680 kN and N_fi,Rd,0 is the design resistance at time zero in fire (using buckling with γ_M,fi = 1.0).
   b. Determine the critical temperature θ_cr from the degree of utilisation.
   c. Using the section factor A_m/V and the standard fire curve (ISO 834), determine whether the unprotected section reaches θ_cr before 60 minutes.
3. For an unprotected steel section, use the incremental temperature rise formula: Δθ_a,t = (A_m/V) × (1 / (c_a × ρ_a)) × h_net × Δt, where c_a ≈ 600 J/(kg·K), ρ_a = 7850 kg/m³.

Part 3 — OPTIMISATION:
The lightest section satisfying ambient buckling may NOT satisfy fire resistance (fire favours heavier sections with lower section factor A_m/V). Find the lightest section satisfying BOTH requirements simultaneously.

Present a comparison table with at least 3 candidate sections showing: section name, mass per metre, area, r_min, λ̄, χ, N_b,Rd (ambient), A_m/V, θ_cr, time to reach θ_cr (unprotected), and pass/fail for both checks.

State your final selected section clearly.
verification_method: Verify: (1) The buckling calculation uses the correct buckling curve for the section type and axis. (2) The fire load is correctly reduced: N_fi,Ed = 0.6 × 2800 = 1680 kN. (3) The section factor A_m/V is correctly computed (typical values for HE sections: 80-200 m⁻¹ — heavier sections have lower values). (4) The critical temperature is correctly derived from the degree of utilisation (θ_cr ≈ 500-600°C for μ_0 ≈ 0.5-0.7). (5) The time to reach critical temperature for an unprotected section is realistically computed (unprotected steel typically reaches 500-600°C in 15-25 minutes — meaning most unprotected sections FAIL R60). This is the key insight: achieving R60 unprotected is extremely difficult and may require a very heavy section.
why_frontier_hard: Two intersecting design codes (EN 1993-1-1 and EN 1993-1-2) with different partial factors, load levels, and failure modes. Models frequently: (1) forget the fire load reduction factor η_fi = 0.6 and check fire at full ambient load, (2) use the wrong buckling curve (using curve 'a' when curve 'b' or 'c' applies), (3) compute A_m/V incorrectly (confusing box perimeter with section perimeter, or forgetting to include the web), (4) fail to recognise that unprotected steel almost never achieves R60 — the honest answer may be that no standard section works unprotected, requiring the model to say so rather than producing a wrong 'solution'. (5) Use section properties from the wrong standard (American W-shapes instead of European HE sections).
